Placental Pathology

Umbilical cord abnormalities, chorionic pathology, molar pregnancy, placenta accreta spectrum, amniotic pathology, infection, and twin placentation.

Umbilical CordChorionMolar PregnancyAccreta SpectrumChorioamnionitis
Image rule
Only cropped gross, histologic, or schematic pathology images from the lecture are shown. Slide text is not used as the teaching image; the explanation is written in the companion.

Lecture map

Umbilical cord: insertion abnormalities, vessel number, thrombosis, knots, and cord length.
Chorion/placenta: calcification, infarction, abruption, hydrops, molar pregnancy, and placenta accreta spectrum.
Amnion/membranes: membrane insertion, meconium changes, chorioamnionitis/funisitis, and twin dividing membranes.

1. Umbilical cord pathology

Normal structural anchor: placental cord vessels are protected by Wharton substance until they branch at the placental insertion. The farther vessels travel without Wharton substance, the more vulnerable they are to compression, thrombosis, or tearing.
Cropped lecture schematic of central/eccentric, marginal, velamentous, and furcate patterns.
InsertionDefinition / locationMain risk emphasized
NormalCentral 2/3 of placental disc; paracentral/eccentric is commonProtected vessels
PeripheralWithin 3 cm of disc edgeMay be less efficient
MarginalWithin 1 cm of disc edgeLess efficient; vessels may extend into membranes
VelamentousCord inserts into membranes; vessels travel through membranes before reaching discCompression or disruption of unprotected vessels
FurcateVessels branch before cord inserts onto chorionic plateNo Wharton protection along branched segments → compression, thrombi, tearing
Cropped gross lecture image: velamentous insertion leaves intramembranous vessels unprotected.
Relationship
The lecture states that all velamentous insertions are furcate, but not all furcate cords are velamentous.

Vessels and cord length

Cropped lecture histology: single umbilical artery. The lecture says to confirm the finding microscopically.

Single umbilical artery

About 20% have additional malformations with significant morbidity/mortality in this lecture. Abnormal karyotype and multiple malformations are more common when the left umbilical artery is missing.

Thrombosis

The lecture associates cord thrombosis with funisitis and true knots.

Long cord >70 cm

Associated with knots, prolapse, and nuchal cord.

Short cord <30 cm

Associated with abruption; in extreme cases the cord may be virtually absent.

2. Chorionic / placental vascular pathology

Calcifications

Multiple white specks on the maternal surface are usually not pathologic according to this lecture.

Infarction

Placental infarcts can be associated with maternal and/or fetal vascular malperfusion. Mature marginal lesions may be difficult to distinguish grossly from intervillous thrombi.

Cropped lecture gross image: placental infarct adjacent to intervillous thrombus.
Hypertensive disease connection
The deck shows multiple infarcts/fibrosis in the context of preeclampsia/eclampsia and later emphasizes that persistence of smooth muscle in central decidua basalis spiral arteries represents failed trophoblast-mediated vascular remodeling.

Placental abruption

Cropped lecture image: retroplacental hematoma and microscopic changes of abruption.

The lecture describes abruption as a retroplacental hematoma adherent to the basal plate, potentially indenting the maternal surface. Fresh lesions can show villous edema, congestion, and hemorrhage; older hematomas may show villous infarction.

Hydropic placenta

Cropped lecture gross image: swollen but recognizable cotyledons in a hydropic placenta.

Lecture associations include Rh incompatibility, TORCH infections, alpha thalassemia, cardiac anomalies, and abnormal fetal karyotype such as Turner syndrome (45,X). The lecture distinguishes generalized hydropic swelling from molar vesicles: cotyledons remain recognizable and there are no separate cysts.

3. Hydatidiform mole: complete vs partial

Fast split: complete mole = no fetus + markedly increased hCG + usually 46XX paternal-only genome; partial mole = fetus/fetal tissue may be present + triploidy + milder hCG elevation.
Cropped gross lecture image: complete mole with cystic villous change and no fetal parts.
Cropped gross lecture image: partial/incomplete mole with fetal tissue present.
FeatureComplete molePartial mole
GeneticsDiploid, androgenetic / paternal only; lecture lists 46XXTriploid; lecture lists 69XXY
FetusAbsentMay be present
hCGMarkedly elevatedSlight/mild elevation
VilliDiffuse enlarged hydropic villi, central cisternsTwo villous populations; irregular large hydropic villi + smaller fibrotic villi
Trophoblast proliferationCircumferentialFocal, no atypia in the lecture summary
p57Lost/negative in villous cytotrophoblasts and stromal cellsRetained/positive
Choriocarcinoma riskLecture states 2–8%Rare / very low
Hydropic villi ≠ automatically mole
The lecture treats hydropic villi as a differential diagnosis for molar pregnancy. Hydropic villi can retain vessels and normal trophoblastic polarity, and p57 is retained.

4. Placenta accreta spectrum

Lecture definition: placenta accreta = direct adherence of chorion to uterus without intervening decidua, causing failure of placental separation at delivery.
Cropped lecture histology showing chorionic villi abutting/invading myometrium.
TermDepth described in lecture
AccretaDirect adherence to uterus without intervening decidua
IncretaChorionic villi invade myometrium
PercretaChorionic villi penetrate transmurally through the uterine wall

5. Amnion and membrane pathology

Membrane insertion

Cropped lecture schematic comparing normal, circummarginate, and circumvallate membrane insertion.
PatternLecture distinction
CircummarginateFibrin ring marks insertion inside disc margin; insertion is flat
CircumvallateInsertion is raised; membranes do not extend to periphery, producing a smaller amnion
Associated consequence shown in lecture
An abnormally small amnion secondary to circumvallate placenta is linked in the deck with fetal flexion deformities.

Meconium

The lecture defines meconium as dark green fetal material and notes that meconium staining is most common in term/post-term deliveries and is debated as a marker of fetal stress. Grossly, cord and membranes may stain green-brown. Histologically, meconium-laden macrophages can appear in amnion, chorion, and umbilical cord stroma.

6. Chorioamnionitis and the amniotic-fluid infection sequence

Most common route in this lecture: ascending infection. The deck lists cervicovaginal flora such as Ureaplasma, E. coli, and Fusobacterium.
Cropped lecture histology: neutrophilic inflammation in acute chorioamnionitis.
Maternal response stageLecture sequence
Stage 1Acute chorionitis and subchorionitis
Stage 2Acute chorioamnionitis
Stage 3Necrotizing acute chorioamnionitis
Fetal response stageLecture sequence
Stage 1Chorionic plate vasculitis and umbilical vein phlebitis
Stage 2Inflammation of one or both umbilical arteries ± phlebitis
Stage 3Necrotizing funisitis with neutrophil arcs toward the surface
Cropped lecture histology: funisitis. The deck defines this as inflammation of the umbilical cord with neutrophils in vessel walls that may extend into Wharton jelly.

Last 30 seconds: velamentous = exposed membranous vessels; complete mole = no fetus / 46XX paternal / high hCG / p57−; partial mole = fetus possible / triploid / p57+; accreta adheres, increta invades myometrium, percreta traverses wall; ascending infection → chorioamnionitis → fetal response/funisitis; twin membrane tells chorionicity.
